commercial context between parties of equal bargaining power (in this case, two corporations).
These early cases did not provide a general rule for assessing whether a provisional remedy comported with the Due Process Clause.
In CONNECTICUT v. DOEHR, p. 286, supra, the Court invalidated a Connecticut statute pursuant to which a judge could allow the
prejudgment attachment of real estate, without prior notice or hearing, upon plaintiff’s assertion under oath that there was probable cause
to sustain the validity of his claims which were unrelated to the property sought to be seized. In place of the ad hoc, multi-factor
approach taken in the Sniadach line of cases, the Court applied the three-part balancing test of MATHEWS v. ELDRIDGE, developed in
the context of disputes concerning eligibility for government benefits. The three-part test considers (1) the private interest that will be
affected by the official action; (2) the risk of an erroneous deprivation of such interest through the procedures used, and probable value, if
any, of additional procedural safeguards; and (3) the government’s interest, including the fiscal and administrative burdens that the
additional or substitute procedures would entail. Four Justices in Doehr stated that, in their view, due process also required the posting of
a bond or some other security, a question that remains open. Compare Diaz v. Paterson, 547 F.3d 88 (2d Cir. 2008), with Tri-State Dev.,
Ltd. v. Johnston, 160 F.3d 528 (9th Cir. 1998). See Beale, Note—Connecticut v. Doehr and Procedural Due Process Values: The
Sniadach Tetrad Revisited, 79 Cornell L.Rev. 1603 (1994); Vandevelde, Ideology, Due Process and Civil Procedure, 67 St. John’s L.Rev.
265, 317–24 (1993).
NOTE AND QUESTIONS
Connecticut amended its prejudgment remedy statute in response to Connecticut v. Doehr. The amended statute requires an evidentiary hearing
before the grant of any prejudgment remedy, but retains the “probable cause” standard for the issuance of relief. Conn. Gen. Statutes § 52–278e. In
HARTFORD ACCIDENT & INDEM. CO. v. ACE AM. REINSUR. CO., 103 Conn. App. 319, 930 A.2d 701 (2007), the state appeals court
considered the constitutionality of Connecticut’s pre-pleading security statute, Conn. Gen. Statutes § 38a–27. Under the statute, an unauthorized
insurance company doing business in the state and sued in the state was required to post security “in an amount to be fixed by the court or the
commissioner sufficient to secure the payment of any final judgment which may be rendered in the action or proceeding.” The statute permitted the
judge or the commissioner, in its discretion, to dispense with the requirement upon a showing that the insurer maintained sufficient funds in the state to
